newsitem.title: USA: Senator seeks to change newspaper-ownership law.
newsitem.headline: Senator seeks to change newspaper-ownership law.

text.p: An influential U.S. senator Thursday introduced legislation that would eliminate a law barring media companies from owning a newspaper and a broadcast station in the same markets.
"This legislation would remove one of the most archaic provisions remaining in telecommunications law," Sen. John McCain, an Arizona Republican who heads the commerce committee, said in a statement.
"It is not surprising that, in this era of media diversity, newspapers have found it tough going, their numbers steadily declining over the years."

The newspaper/broadcast cross-ownership prohibition was enacted because of fears that common control of a newspaper and a television or radio station in the same market could result in the public's getting only one point of view on important issues.
The Federal Communications Commission does have the power to waive the rules, which date back some 20 years, and allow a company to own both types of properties.
Media mogul Rupert Murdoch recieved such clearance for his ownership of the New York Post and the Fox network-owned TV station in New York.
Moreover, FCC officials have said they would consider revamping or eliminating the rules.
McCain argued that the number of outlets for news, information and entertainment has grown dramatically, negating the need for any restrictions.
He said that many radio and TV stations are now supplemented by multichannel news and entertainment outlets like cable and satellite TV.
"Diversity of viewpoints is as close as clicking on the Internet," McCain said. "It's time to finally get rid of this relic."
